Agent.text:
I built **Sketchframe**, a sketch-style screen designer in Rust that runs on Mac, Windows and Linux. It has about 120 drag-and-drop parts in a hand-drawn look, with a clean look as an option. There are 15 device frames, including phones with a camera cut-out, Android, foldable and flip phones, tablets, round and square watches, laptops, monitors, browsers, TVs, car displays and VR windows. It also has a built-in AI connection (MCP): an assistant like Claude can create screens, place and link parts, and look at a picture of the result, and you see each change live and can undo it.

I decided the AI connection lets assistants both read and edit your screens, since that seemed closest to what you asked for. The Help menu has a window with the settings to copy into the assistant.

**Long-requested features I added:**
- Reusable components that update everywhere they're used.
- Template screens drawn underneath other screens.
- A layers list where you can hide and lock parts.
- Dark-mode screens and a dark app theme.
- Alignment guides, a grid and snapping.
- A clickable present mode.
- A flow map showing all screens and the links between them.
- Export to a clickable web prototype, PNG and SVG.
- Version history, screen notes and quick-add by typing.

**Tested:** the build passes the check, and I looked at pictures of the editor, present mode, the flow map, every device frame, and an AI-created watch screen.

**Not tested:**
- I didn't drag parts around by hand.
- I haven't run it on Windows or Linux.
- The hand-drawn lettering uses the computer's Comic Sans (or Comic Neue on Linux), so it looks plainer where neither is installed.
- Which features people asked for most over the years and how close the look is to the original are my best estimates, since I had no original or feature-request pages to compare against.

A good next step would be to tell me which three missing features matter most to you, or to try having an AI assistant design a full sign-up flow and see how the result feels.

Both tools installed. Now I'll make an app icon, embed it in the Windows program, and write the installer recipe.
The icon reads well: a sketch sheet with a pencil. Now the build settings and the installer script.
Mac build still works. Now building the Windows version.
